questions.question: What does clock.getDelta() return in a Three.js game loop?
options: The total number of frames rendered since the clock was created
The current timestamp in milliseconds since the page loaded
The elapsed time in seconds since the last call to getDelta()
The current frame rate as frames per second
questions.explanation: getDelta() returns the time in seconds since it was last called. At 60 FPS this is about 0.016, at 30 FPS about 0.033. Multiplying movement by this value makes speed frame-rate independent.

questions.question: A player moves with: player.position.z -= 8 * delta. What does this guarantee?
options: The player moves exactly 8 pixels toward the camera every frame
The player moves at 8 Three.js units per second regardless of frame rate
The player rotates 8 degrees per second around the Z axis
The player reaches position z = -8 after exactly one second only at 60 FPS
questions.explanation: Multiplying by delta converts per-frame movement into per-second movement. 8 * 0.016 = 0.128 units at 60 FPS; 8 * 0.033 = 0.264 units at 30 FPS — both sum to approximately 8 units per second.

questions.question: Why is polling (maintaining a 'keys' object) better than using only keydown events for smooth game movement?
options: keydown events fire faster than polling on high-refresh-rate displays
Polling uses less memory than registering event listeners
keydown fires once with OS key-repeat delay; polling reads the held state every frame for smooth continuous movement
Event listeners cannot detect arrow keys in browsers, only letter keys
questions.explanation: The OS fires keydown once immediately, then again after a delay, then repeatedly. Polling reads whether the key is currently held on every frame, giving smooth movement without the initial stutter caused by OS key-repeat.

questions.question: AABB collision detection gives an incorrect result when:
options: One of the objects is a Three.js Mesh rather than a Group
Both objects are at the same Y position on the ground
The scene contains more than 20 simultaneous AABB checks
The objects are rotating, since AABB assumes axis-aligned (non-rotating) bounding boxes
questions.explanation: AABB stands for Axis-Aligned Bounding Box. The boxes must remain aligned with the world axes. Rotated objects extend beyond their bounding box corners, causing missed or incorrect collision results.

questions.question: What is the main reason to use a physics engine like Rapier.js instead of manual AABB for a game?
options: Rapier handles gravity, friction, joints, and complex collider shapes that manual AABB cannot simulate
Rapier renders geometry faster than the Three.js WebGLRenderer
AABB does not work in browsers — it only runs in Node.js environments
Manual collision detection requires a paid Three.js Pro license for production use
questions.explanation: Manual AABB is limited to non-rotating box-shaped objects. Rapier handles rigid body simulation with gravity, forces, multiple collider shapes (spheres, capsules, convex hulls), joints, and continuous collision detection.
